newsitem.title: UK: Low-grade bureaucrats die younger, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Low-grade bureaucrats die younger, study finds.

text.p: Civil servants who never make the grade and do not get perks such as cars are more likely to die soon after retirement than their bosses, British researchers reported on Friday.
The findings add to a growing body of evidence linking socio-economic status with health.
Michael Marmot and Martin Shipley at University College London's medical school studied more than 18,000 men who worked in the British civil service.
They found that those on lower grades died sooner after retirement than the men who reached higher rank.

"Overall, 30 percent of men in the administrative grade died during the 25-year followup compared with 69 percent of men in the lowest grade," Marmot and Shipley wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
Having perks seemed to help survival, they found.

"Lack of ownership of a car was associated with a 57 percent higher mortality before retirement and 34 percent higher mortality after retirement." Marmot and Shipley's report did not go into the possible reasons, although other studies have shown that men of lower socio-economic status not only tend to be less healthy, but seem to be suffer more from stress.
"Work itself may play an important part in generating social inequalities in health in men of working age," they said.
